title: Building a Consistent Quiet Time as a Busy Dad
meta_description: A quiet time for a busy dad has to survive sick kids and 6 a.m. practices. Here's how to build one that bends without breaking.
body_markdown:
## The problem isn't your discipline

Most advice about a daily quiet time assumes you control your mornings. If you have young kids, you don't. Your schedule is set by whoever wakes up first, whoever threw up at 2 a.m., whoever has a 6:45 practice across town.

So you build a plan around a quiet house at 5:30. It works for nine days. Then a kid gets croup, you lose a week, and you conclude the problem is you.

It usually isn't. The problem is a definition of consistency borrowed from fitness culture: same time, every day, unbroken chain. That definition was built for people whose time is their own. A father's time belongs, in large part, to other people. That's not a failure of the spiritual life. It's the shape of it.

## Redefine consistency as returning

Here's a more honest standard: consistency isn't never missing. It's always coming back.

A dad who reads Scripture four mornings one week, one morning the next, and then seven the week after is consistent in the way that matters. He hasn't drifted. He hasn't decided it's not for him. He keeps returning to the same place.

If you measure yourself by the unbroken chain, every interruption becomes a verdict. If you measure yourself by returning, every interruption becomes something you simply walk back from.

## Anchor to an event, not a clock

A time on the clock is fragile. An event is sturdier.

Instead of "5:30 a.m.," try "before I check my phone" or "while the coffee brews" or "in the car before I walk into work." Events move with your day. If the baby wakes at 4:50 instead of 6:00, "while the coffee brews" still happens. "5:30" doesn't.

Pick the one moment in your day that survives almost anything. For a lot of fathers, that's the drive to work or the ten minutes after the kids are finally down. It doesn't have to be dawn. It has to be reliable.

## Shrink the unit until it's unbreakable

If your plan requires 30 minutes, it will fail on any morning that only offers eight. Build the plan for the eight-minute morning and let the longer ones be a gift.

That might mean one chapter. Some days it means one paragraph, read slowly, twice. You'd be surprised how much a single paragraph of Romans or a single psalm holds when you're not trying to get through it.

The goal is a unit so small you'd feel a little silly skipping it.

## Stay in one passage all week

Reading plans that move you to a new chapter every day quietly punish the dad who misses Tuesday and Wednesday. Now he's behind, and behind feels like guilt.

Try this instead: one passage for the whole week. Monday you read it. Tuesday you read it again and notice something new. Thursday you missed Wednesday and it doesn't matter, because you're still in the same place. By Sunday you know it in a way daily skimming never produces.

This is how Scripture was carried for most of history: slowly, repeatedly, often out loud. It's also how a tired mind actually retains things.

## Let the interruptions in

When your four-year-old wanders in mid-psalm, you have two options. Treat it as the moment your quiet time ended, or treat it as the moment it changed shape.

Read the rest out loud with him on your lap. He won't understand most of it. He'll understand that this is what his dad does in the morning. That is not a lesser version of the practice. For a father, it may be the truest one.

## Stop counting

A lot of Bible apps will show you a streak number, and a lot of men quietly organize their reading around not losing it. When the streak breaks, the motivation goes with it.

This is part of why Selah was built without streaks or badges. The app opens to the text and a moment of quiet, and that's it. There's nothing to protect, nothing to lose on the morning a kid is sick. You open it, you read, you close it. The next time you open it, it doesn't remind you how long you were gone.

For a busy dad, that absence matters more than any feature. The point was never the number. The point was to keep showing up to the Word, at whatever hour the day allows, and to be able to walk back to it without shame when the day allows nothing.

## A realistic week

Pick one passage. Pick one event you can anchor to. Set the unit at one paragraph. Read it every day you can, out loud if there's someone on your lap.

When you miss, don't restart. Just return.
